title: Hamlet
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act I, Scene I — Elsinore. A platform before the castle.
about:
At Elsinore, the guards are watching for a ghost. Hamlet, son of the dead king, mourns his father and is disturbed by his mother’s marriage to the king’s brother, Claudius. When the ghost describes a murder and demands revenge, Hamlet must judge both the message and its messenger. Can he trust a spirit? What would count as proof? And who will be harmed when he acts?

This is more than the story of a man who delays. Hamlet investigates, performs, mocks, threatens, and acts suddenly as well as reflectively. Others watch him and try to direct him. Conversations become traps, affectionate advice can lead to surveillance, and a performance becomes an attempt to uncover a crime. Horatio, Ophelia, Laertes, and Gertrude each have a place in a conflict Hamlet cannot control alone.

Read it as a play: notice who is present, who listens unseen, and who speaks only to the audience. Public speech, private thought, songs, and the players’ speeches sound different. The text is arranged in five acts and twenty scenes.

angleCards.title: Who knows what?
angleCards.text: The ghost’s story, the king’s reactions, and the conversations behind tapestries provide different kinds of evidence. Distinguish what you see as a reader from what any one character can know.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how suspicion becomes conviction and what evidence people use to justify their decisions.

angleCards.title: Playing a part
angleCards.text: Hamlet announces an intention to act mad. That does not make every feeling a performance or every action part of a plan. Compare his conversations with his friends, his soliloquies, and his treatment of Ophelia.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine performance, grief, and loss of control without deciding their boundaries in advance.

angleCards.title: The consequences of revenge
angleCards.text: Hamlet, Laertes, and Fortinbras are each connected with a father’s legacy. Their responses differ. Watch who demands revenge, who tries to direct it, and who pays its costs.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare revenge with responsibility and see how one action changes other people’s choices.

angleCards.title: Words doing several jobs
angleCards.text: A pun may flirt, insult, evade, or threaten. Images of disease, acting, ears, and poison recur. Listen for changes in register, especially when a character borrows or mocks another person’s language.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to hear the different voices and track the images people use to understand and influence one another.

cast.name: Hamlet
cast.description: Son of the dead king and Gertrude. A student at Wittenberg, he wants to understand what happened to his father. Wit and reflection coexist with grief, cruelty, and impulsive action.

cast.name: Claudius
cast.description: The old king’s brother and Gertrude’s new husband. Labelled KING in the dialogue, he seeks to protect both the kingdom and his own position as Hamlet’s behavior arouses suspicion.

cast.name: Gertrude
cast.description: Hamlet’s mother and Claudius’s wife, bound to both her son and her new husband. What she knows at each point should be inferred from her words and reactions rather than assumed in advance.

cast.name: The Ghost
cast.description: Appears in the form of the old King Hamlet and calls for revenge. Its account of murder and the afterlife begins the action, but Hamlet also questions what kind of spirit he has encountered.

cast.name: Ophelia
cast.description: Has received Hamlet’s declarations of love. Her father and brother warn her against him, and the court’s investigation of the prince intrudes on their relationship. Her later songs connect love, loss, and mourning.

cast.name: Polonius
cast.description: Father of Ophelia and Laertes. He gives elaborate advice and gathers information through questions and hidden observation. What happens onstage often tests his confident explanations.

cast.name: Laertes
cast.description: Ophelia’s brother, who travels to France and later returns. His family loyalties and demand for redress offer an important comparison with Hamlet’s.

cast.name: Horatio
cast.description: A scholar who sees the ghost and becomes Hamlet’s confidant. He helps observe, remember, and eventually recount what has happened.

cast.name: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern
cast.description: Summoned by the king and queen to keep Hamlet company and discover the cause of his change. Friendship and service to the court come to pull in different directions.

cast.name: Fortinbras
cast.description: Nephew of Norway’s present king and son of the Fortinbras defeated by the old King Hamlet. His military plans give the Danish court’s conflict an external setting.

cast.name: The players, gravediggers, and Osric
cast.description: The players display the force of emotion and performance. The gravediggers joke about death, rank, and law. The courtier Osric’s elaborate speech immediately invites Hamlet’s mockery.

whyItMatters.title: Thought changing as we hear it
whyItMatters.body: Hamlet’s soliloquies do not simply announce finished opinions. They test possibilities, accuse him, and change direction. His later actions have no simple relationship to those thoughts. The play makes this movement visible without giving one explanation that fits every choice.

whyItMatters.title: A court of watchers
whyItMatters.body: People watch one another, hide, interpret letters, and turn others into experiments. The play-within-the-play concentrates that pattern: a staged action is meant to reveal something, but its audience does not necessarily understand it in the same way. Readers also judge signs whose meaning the characters dispute.

whyItMatters.title: Grief and power beyond the prince
whyItMatters.body: The royal family’s conflict harms people around it. Ophelia and Laertes show that Hamlet’s grief is not the play’s only grief. Questions of monarchy, popular support, and war continue alongside it. Personal and political consequences remain closely connected.

openingText: [Enter Francisco and Barnardo, two sentinels] BARNARDO. Who's there? FRANCISCO. No — you answer me first. Stop and identify yourself. BARNARDO. Long live the King! FRANCISCO. Barnardo? BARNARDO. That's me. FRANCISCO. You're right on time for your shift. BARNARDO. It's just struck midnight. Get yourself to bed, Francisco.
